segments.text: Watch parallel rays pass through two curved glass surfaces and crowd toward a common focus.
segments.say: Watch parallel rays pass through two curved glass surfaces and crowd toward a common focus.

segments.text: Now zoom in. The outer rays cross before the central rays, so one point cannot catch them all.
segments.say: Now zoom in. The outer rays cross before the central rays, so one point cannot catch them all.

segments.text: How can we predict this mismatch without pretending a real lens is infinitely thin?
segments.say: How can we predict this mismatch without pretending a real lens is infinitely thin?

segments.text: Trace each ray: find the next surface, change its direction, then repeat.
segments.say: Trace each ray: find the next surface, change its direction, then repeat.

segments.text: A ray marks a local direction of light travel. It is not the complete electric field.
segments.say: A ray marks a local direction of light travel. It is not the complete electric field.

segments.text: Store a starting position and a unit direction vector. Distance along that direction is our variable.
segments.say: Store a starting position and a unit direction vector. Distance along that direction is our variable.

segments.text: In uniform material, a ray follows a straight line. A boundary can change its direction.
segments.say: In uniform material, a ray follows a straight line. A boundary can change its direction.

segments.text: Our lens has two spherical surfaces, four millimetres apart, with glass index one point five.
segments.say: Our lens has two spherical surfaces, four millimetres apart, with glass index one point five.

segments.text: You see a central slice of a three-dimensional calculation. The optical axis runs horizontally, along z.
segments.say: You see a central slice of a three-dimensional calculation. The optical axis runs horizontally, along zee.

segments.text: Curvature, thickness, and aperture specify the glass. We still need to calculate where light goes.
segments.say: Curvature, thickness, and aperture specify the glass. We still need to calculate where light goes.

segments.text: First, extend the incoming line until it meets the first spherical surface. Calculate that intersection.
segments.say: First, extend the incoming line until it meets the first spherical surface. Calculate that intersection.

segments.text: Substitute the ray into the sphere equation. A quadratic gives two possible roots, one, or none.
segments.say: Substitute the ray into the sphere equation. A quadratic gives two possible roots, one, or none.

segments.text: But our optical surface is only a spherical cap. A root on the opposite cap must be rejected.
segments.say: But our optical surface is only a spherical cap. A root on the opposite cap must be rejected.

segments.text: Keep a forward intersection on the correct cap, inside the clear aperture. Otherwise, report a missed surface.
segments.say: Keep a forward intersection on the correct cap, inside the clear aperture. Otherwise, report a missed surface.

segments.text: At the accepted point, construct the normal. For a sphere, it follows the line through its centre.
segments.say: At the accepted point, construct the normal. For a sphere, it follows the line through its centre.

segments.text: Orient the normal into the next medium. Measure bending from this local direction, not from the optical axis.
segments.say: Orient the normal into the next medium. Measure bending from this local direction, not from the optical axis.

segments.text: Split the incoming unit direction into parts tangent and normal to the interface.
segments.say: Split the incoming unit direction into parts tangent and normal to the interface.

segments.text: The phase variation along that interface must match on both sides. That determines the tangential part.
segments.say: The phase variation along that interface must match on both sides. That determines the tangential part.

segments.text: Divide the first refractive index by the second. Multiply the tangential direction by this ratio.
segments.say: Divide the first refractive index by the second. Multiply the tangential direction by this ratio.

segments.text: From air into glass, the ratio is below one. The ray bends toward the normal.
segments.say: From air into glass, the ratio is below one. The ray bends toward the normal.

segments.text: Rebuild the normal component to make a unit vector. Choose the branch entering the next medium.
segments.say: Rebuild the normal component to make a unit vector. Choose the branch entering the next medium.

segments.text: This is vector Snell refraction. The familiar sine law describes the same rule using angles.
segments.say: This is vector Snell refraction. The familiar sine law describes the same rule using angles.

segments.text: From glass into air, the tangential part grows. Beyond the critical angle, no real transmitted direction exists.
segments.say: From glass into air, the tangential part grows. Beyond the critical angle, no real transmitted direction exists.

segments.text: That is total internal reflection. Our transmitted path stops; following the reflected branch requires another trace.
segments.say: That is total internal reflection. Our transmitted path stops; following the reflected branch requires another trace.

segments.text: Find the second surface using the new direction. A thick lens requires two separate refractions.
segments.say: Find the second surface using the new direction. A thick lens requires two separate refractions.

segments.text: Recompute the normal and exchange the refractive indices. This time, the ray leaves glass for air.
segments.say: Recompute the normal and exchange the refractive indices. This time, the ray leaves glass for air.

segments.text: Intersect the outgoing line with a detector plane. This point is the ray's predicted landing position.
segments.say: Intersect the outgoing line with a detector plane. This point is the ray's predicted landing position.

segments.text: Repeat across the entrance aperture. Every path shown comes from surface intersections and Snell refraction.
segments.say: Repeat across the entrance aperture. Every path shown comes from surface intersections and Snell refraction.

segments.text: Near the axis, ray angles are small. Linearizing their motion gives the paraxial focus, marked here.
segments.say: Near the axis, ray angles are small. Linearizing their motion gives the paraxial focus, marked here.

segments.text: That focus is a useful reference, not a promise for every ray through a finite lens.
segments.say: That focus is a useful reference, not a promise for every ray through a finite lens.

segments.text: Open the aperture without changing the lens. Outer rays now sample steeper surface regions.
segments.say: Open the aperture without changing the lens. Outer rays now sample steeper surface regions.

segments.text: Watch the enlarged focus. For this spherical lens, outer rays cross the axis before central rays.
segments.say: Watch the enlarged focus. For this spherical lens, outer rays cross the axis before central rays.

segments.text: This mismatch is spherical aberration. It comes from the geometry, not a coarse numerical grid.
segments.say: This mismatch is spherical aberration. It comes from the geometry, not a coarse numerical grid.

segments.text: Move the detector. The bundle narrows and spreads, but its rays never all meet.
segments.say: Move the detector. The bundle narrows and spreads, but its rays never all meet.

segments.text: Here, best focus minimizes the root mean square distance from the spot centroid. Other criteria can differ.
segments.say: Here, best focus minimizes the root mean square distance from the spot centroid. Other criteria can differ.

segments.text: Tilt the input. The off-axis pattern changes, so an on-axis test cannot describe the whole image.
segments.say: Tilt the input. The off-axis pattern changes, so an on-axis test cannot describe the whole image.

segments.text: Closing the aperture reduces geometric spread but rejects light. A smaller ray spot is not the whole story.
segments.say: Closing the aperture reduces geometric spread but rejects light. A smaller ray spot is not the whole story.

segments.text: These are geometric paths. Their landing points are not a diffraction point spread function.
segments.say: These are geometric paths. Their landing points are not a diffraction point spread function.

segments.text: Waves still spread through a finite aperture, as in episode three. Closing the aperture can increase diffraction blur.
segments.say: Waves still spread through a finite aperture, as in episode three. Closing the aperture can increase diffraction blur.

segments.text: Our ideal surfaces use one fixed index. We omit reflected power, dispersion, absorption, and manufacturing errors.
segments.say: Our ideal surfaces use one fixed index. We omit reflected power, dispersion, absorption, and manufacturing errors.

segments.text: A missed surface or total internal reflection is a tracing outcome. Check those before comparing image errors.
segments.say: A missed surface or total internal reflection is a tracing outcome. Check those before comparing image errors.

segments.text: Other surface shapes use the same logic. More rays sample the chosen model more densely; they do not add missing physics.
segments.say: Other surface shapes use the same logic. More rays sample the chosen model more densely; they do not add missing physics.

segments.text: One ray follows one recipe: intersect, construct the normal, refract, and continue.
segments.say: One ray follows one recipe: intersect, construct the normal, refract, and continue.

segments.text: A bundle reveals the consequences. Aperture, field angle, and detector position all affect the geometric image.
segments.say: A bundle reveals the consequences. Aperture, field angle, and detector position all affect the geometric image.

segments.text: The paraxial focus starts the design. Exact surface tracing tests the finite lens within its assumptions.
segments.say: The paraxial focus starts the design. Exact surface tracing tests the finite lens within its assumptions.

segments.text: Next, we will choose lens shapes using image error, while keeping the required focal length.
segments.say: Next, we will choose lens shapes using image error, while keeping the required focal length.
